account: On 2 January 2015 the Southern Nevada Health District began a controlled experiment with nEmesis, a University of Rochester system. It applies a language model built on a support vector machine to geotagged tweets and ranks Las Vegas food venues by their risk of foodborne illness. During the first three months environmental health specialists inspected 142 venues. Half were chosen by nEmesis and half under the standard protocol. Inspectors were blind to which was which. Inspections guided by nEmesis, which the authors call adaptive inspections, uncovered 9 demerits per inspection versus 6 (p = 0.019). They found 11 venues graded C or worse versus 7 for controls. The authors call this a 64% improvement, and their abstract summarizes it as 63% more effective. Side findings included an unpermitted seafood establishment and a food handler working with an influenza-like illness. The health district performed 5 foodborne-illness investigations between 2 January and 31 March 2015, against 11 in the same window the year before. The authors estimate, from outbreak averages of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, that adaptive inspections saved 71 infections and 4.4 hospitalizations over the three months. They estimate that making all of the more than 35,000 annual inspections in Las Vegas adaptive could prevent more than 9,126 cases and 557 hospitalizations a year. In 2016 the same health district tested FINDER, a different model built by Google. The developers published a journal version of the nEmesis study in AI Magazine on 31 March 2017 that gives the gain as 64 percent. On 6 November 2018 the FINDER authors reported that 52.3% of the 132 venues that FINDER chose in Las Vegas and Chicago were unsafe, against 24.7% of other inspections.

So the difference in findings is attributable to the AI's venue selection. The developers (Rochester) are distinct from the deployer (SNHD), though SNHD staff co-authored the paper. The paper was peer-reviewed as an IAAI deployed paper.

They estimate that making all of the more than 35,000 annual inspections in Las Vegas adaptive could prevent more than 9,126 cases and 557 hospitalizations a year. In 2016 the same health district tested FINDER, a different model built by Google. The developers published a journal version of the nEmesis study in AI Magazine on 31 March 2017 that gives the gain as 64 percent. On 6 November 2018 the FINDER authors reported that 52.3% of the 132 venues that FINDER chose in Las Vegas and Chicago were unsafe, against 24.7% of other inspections.

purpose: Rank Las Vegas food venues by predicted foodborne-illness risk, inferred from Twitter posts, so that health inspectors can prioritize the riskiest venues.

ratings.reason: In 142 blinded inspections the nEmesis arm found 9 versus 6 demerits per inspection (p = 0.019). It found 11 versus 7 venues graded C or worse, an unpermitted seafood establishment and a sick food handler.

The 71 infections and 4.4 hospitalizations said to be saved are the authors' estimates from outbreak averages of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The drop in foodborne-illness investigations from 11 to 5 comes from an uncontrolled comparison with the year before, so no prevented illness is measured.
